prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, opening a new regime of measurement precision

statement.case_for: B009 has the broadest agreement in this room: three first-place rankings, six top-three and all eight members ranking it. The substance justifies that. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the dominant systematic of a trapped-atom clock and so allows many atoms to be interrogated at once, which gives the statistical power needed for uncertainties near 1e-18. Ye's group carried the idea to the systematic frontier and to many-body clock physics. The result is the most accurate measurement made in any field, independently reproduced in Sr and Yb at several national laboratories and intercompared across continents. It underlies tests of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is clean, and the prize is a clear case of an invention that extends what can be measured and how accurately.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control) already cover the neighbouring lineage, so a clock prize could look like a third helping from precision atomic physics, and some will call it metrology engineering rather than a discovery. Credit is also not airtight: Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Gill and others demonstrated key milestones, and a Ye-heavy attribution could understate the roles of the Yb and Hg communities and of the ion-clock groups. Finally, if the redefinition of the second is the real outcome, the committee may prefer to wait for it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B009 first and stresses that the idea, its realisation and the statistical-metrology payoff from many atoms and low quantum projection noise are crisp, and that other lattice-clock groups and earlier ion-clock and comb work may be argued as part of the credit.
responses.response: I agree with the statistical-metrology argument, which is the physical reason the lattice works: Katori's trapping idea makes parallel interrogation possible, and the stability follows from that. On the comb and ion-clock lineage, I think it should be handled in the citation, not by widening the prize. The comb is the clockwork and the ion clock is a different route to accuracy, whereas the invention here is magic-wavelength confinement of neutral atoms. Adding Yb or Hg groups would exceed what a three-person limit allows, and the founding idea is Katori's.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first, but also lists B009 second. His reservations are whether the committee should anchor on the diffuse-flux discovery or wait for firmer source identification, and whether lattice clocks are a precision-engineering achievement or a discovery-class advance.
responses.response: I take the engineering-versus-discovery question seriously, but I do not think it separates these two cases as cleanly as stated. IceCube is also instrument-driven, and its source identification is still at moderate significance (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the galactic plane). Clock accuracy is a settled, reproduced measurement result with demonstrated reach into fundamental physics. If the committee wants a discovery framing, I would point to the gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, and to the clock comparisons that now constrain dark-matter and constant-variation models. I still prefer B009 now, though I accept B052 may deserve a prize soon.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first and the topological insulator candidate second, and ranks the lattice clock only fifth. He argues that a new observational window is the kind of finding nature itself delivers, and that credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the precursors, and the choice between detector concept, 2013 discovery and source identification, is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that opening a window is a strong criterion, and the diffuse flux is firmly established. My disagreement is that the unresolved questions you raise, the three-person limit against a large collaboration and the AMANDA and Baikal precursors, are exactly the attribution problems that B009 does not have. Katori and Ye are two identifiable people with a clean split between idea and realisation. I would not rank B052 below clocks on merit; I rank it below on attribution and on how far source identification has matured.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B009 first and notes that the atomic-structure input behind the clock transitions is physics that rewards study, while worrying whether the committee sees the clock as distinct enough from earlier comb and ion-clock recognition and whether the priority between concept and early experiments can be settled.
responses.response: Largely agreed. On priority, the proposal precedes the first demonstrations and the later accuracy milestones, so the sequence supports Katori for the concept and the strontium demonstration, and Ye for the performance. On distinctness, I would stress that magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms is a different invention from either the comb or the ion trap, even if I would not dismiss the committee's concern about cumulative atomic-physics prizes. I think it is answered by the citation wording rather than by changing the configuration.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the Cirac-Zoller proposals second, and acknowledges that circuit QED is his own field and that following the 2025 circuit prize with another superconducting-circuit award may be unbalanced.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and share the concern about balance after 2025, which is also a reason I do not push B008 above clocks. On B014, I agree the pair is clean, but it would be a theory-only award, and the 2012 prize already recognised the experimental realisation of ion control. That is a real qualification, not a reason to dismiss it. It makes B014 a good alternative, not the lead candidate in this round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the clock as a discovery-class advance or as instrumentation after the 2005 and 2012 atomic-physics prizes.
How much weight the redefinition of the second should carry, and whether to wait for it.
Relative credit of Katori and Ye versus Yb, Hg and ion-clock groups outside the credited names; I rely on my recollection of the history and have not verified it here.
Whether B018 or B014 should be advanced if the committee prefers a prize outside precision atomic physics.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: Jun Ye trained in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, where I also spent a research period during my doctoral studies, and I work in the same broad field of atomic physics and laser spectroscopy at Lund. I regard this as a disclosed professional connection, not a stake in the outcome, though the committee may wish to consider it. I also work on quantum memories and the Cirac-Zoller area (B014) is adjacent to my field. I have no documented direct collaboration with Katori or Ye.
